t: GCD Sort of an Array: Union-Find on Prime Factors
o: Swapping is legal precisely between values sharing a common factor greater than 1, and legality composes transitively: if value a can trade into position b and b into c, then a can effectively reach c. In [7,21,3] all three values interconnect via shared factors 7 and 3, so sorting succeeds; in [5,2,6,2] the isolated 5 makes sorting impossible. The question therefore reduces to connectivity: for every index i, nums[i] must be connected to sorted(nums)[i]. With n up to 30000 but values capped at 100000, comparing all pairs costs about 450 million gcd computations and is too slow, while sieving primes up to 100000 is cheap.
k: The gcd-based swap rule generates an equivalence relation: two values are chain-connected exactly when a path of shared prime factors links them.
Routing connections through primes themselves, unioning each element with its distinct prime factors, replaces O(n^2) pairwise edges with O(n log V) unions.
The array is sortable if and only if nums[i] and sorted(nums)[i] lie in the same component for every i.
A smallest-prime-factor sieve factorizes any value up to 10^5 in O(log V) by repeated division.

a.n: Approach 1: Explicit Swap Graph + Connected Components
a.i: Model indices as graph nodes with an edge whenever gcd of the values exceeds 1, then compute connected components with BFS or DFS. Within one component, adjacent swaps can rearrange values arbitrarily, like bubble sort on a fully connected group. Sortability then means each component can be filled with exactly the multiset of values the sorted array demands at those positions.
s: Build adjacency lists, connecting every pair (i, j) whose values share gcd > 1.
Label components via BFS from every unvisited node.
Group the array values by component and sort each group.
Walk positions left to right, matching sorted groups against the globally sorted target.
Return true only if every position matches.
a.t: O(n^2 log V) to test and build all pairs plus BFS over O(n^2) edges; correct but unusable at n = 3*10^4.

a.n: Approach 2: SPF Sieve + DSU over Prime Factors
a.i: Two values are chain-connected exactly when some sequence of shared primes links them, so edges can be routed through the primes themselves: union every element with each distinct prime factor it contains. This slashes the work to O(n log V) unions. A smallest-prime-factor sieve factorizes each value quickly, and the final check compares roots of nums[i] and sorted(nums)[i].
s: Sieve the smallest prime factor spf[v] for all v up to max(nums).
Initialize union-find over the value range [0, max(nums)].
For each element x, strip primes p via spf repeatedly and union(x, p) for each distinct p.
Sort a copy of the array as the target.
Return true iff find(nums[i]) equals find(target[i]) for every i.
a.t: O(V log log V + n log V + n log n) covering the sieve, per-element factorization with near-constant amortized unions, and the final sort.
a.sp: O(V) for the sieve and DSU arrays over the value range V = max(nums).

w: Frame the problem as connectivity first, then choose how to build components. Pitfalls: assuming adjacent sorted values must be directly swappable (transitivity through shared primes is what matters), comparing roots before all unions are done, and forgetting equal values trivially satisfy the check. Mention that trial division up to sqrt(10^5), about 316, is a fine substitute when a sieve feels heavy. Follow-ups: dynamic insertions with an online DSU, or value ranges too large for a sieve where Pollard-rho factorization takes over.
